mainTopic: The end of סנחריב, אברהם's war with the kings, and the reward for נבוכדנצר's four steps
overview: This amud finishes the אגדה about סנחריב. הקב"ה has him disguised, his hair and beard are burned off as ישעיהו foretold, and his own sons kill him while he worships a plank from נח's תיבה. The גמרא then explains words in the פסוק about אברהם's war with the kings. רבי יוחנן and רבי יצחק נפחא argue whether 'לילה' is an angel's name or means the stars fought for him. רבי יוחנן also says אברהם weakened at דן because he foresaw idol worship there. After a remark from רבי זירא, the גמרא brings ירמיה's question of why the wicked succeed, and Heaven's answer through a parable of a tired runner. The point is that if נבוכדנצר earned great reward for just four steps taken for God's honor, the reward of the אבות will be far greater. The גמרא tells the story of those four steps: נבוכדנצר insisted God be named first in a letter to חזקיהו, ran to fix it, and was stopped by גבריאל. It ends by explaining the name 'בלאדן בן בלאדן' and the פסוק 'a son honors his father and a servant his master,' which continues on the next amud.

steps.title: סנחריב is told to disguise himself and sent for scissors
steps.stepSummary: הקב"ה tells סנחריב to change his appearance and sends him to a house for scissors, where he finds מלאכי השרת disguised as men grinding date pits.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'And change yourself.' סנחריב asked: With what should I change? He said: Go bring Me scissors and I will shave you Myself. From where should I bring them? Go into that house and bring them. He went and found מלאכי השרת who looked to him like men, and they were grinding date pits.
steps.whatsHappening: The story of סנחריב continues. הקב"ה tells him to disguise himself, and he is sent to a house where angels in human form are grinding date pits.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier, סנחריב was afraid the kings whose sons died in his army would recognize him and take revenge. The disguise is a haircut. It sets up the humiliating shaving that comes next.

phrases.english: and change yourself.
phrases.notes: הקב"ה is still talking to סנחריב, telling him to disguise himself so the kings won't recognize him.

phrases.english: With what shall I change?

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: זִיל אַיְיתִי לִי מַסְפְּרָא
phrases.english: He said to him: Go bring me scissors
and I will shave you Myself.
From where should I bring them?

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: עוּל לְהָהוּא בֵּיתָא וְאַיְיתֵי.
phrases.english: He said to him: Go into that house and bring them.
He went and found ministering angels,
and they appeared to him like men,
and they were grinding date pits.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the סנחריב story from the previous daf.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: סנחריב is told to disguise himself and is sent to disguised angels for scissors.

steps.title: סנחריב works for the scissors, and fire burns off his hair and beard
steps.stepSummary: The angels make סנחריב grind a סאה of pits before giving him scissors. By then it is dark. He is sent for fire, and while fanning it the fire catches his beard and burns off his head and beard hair.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said: Give me scissors. They said: Grind one סאה of pits and we will give them to you. He ground one סאה of pits and they gave him scissors. By the time he came back it was dark. They said: Go bring fire. He went and brought fire. While he was blowing on it, the fire caught his beard. It spread and shaved off his head and his beard.
steps.whatsHappening: The great king is made to do slave work grinding pits. Then he accidentally burns off all his hair while blowing on a fire.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The story shows סנחריב being humiliated step by step: first menial labor, then losing his hair and beard by his own fire. This sets up the פסוק quoted in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: A סאה, a measure of dry volume

phrases.english: He said to them: Give me scissors.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַרוּ לֵיהּ: טְחוֹן חַד גְּרִיוָא דְּקַשְׁיָיתָא
phrases.english: They said to him: Grind one se'a of pits
and we will give them to you.
He ground one se'a of pits
and they gave him scissors.
By the time he came back, it grew dark.
They said to him: Go bring fire.
He went and brought fire.
While he was blowing on it,
the fire caught onto his beard.
It spread and sheared off his head and his beard.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the scissors episode to its outcome.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: סנחריב's head and beard are burned off by his own fire.

steps.title: The פסוק about the beard is fulfilled
steps.stepSummary: The story is tied to ישעיהו's prophecy that the beard would be destroyed.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said: This is what is written: 'And it shall also sweep away the beard.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows that the burning of סנחריב's beard is what the פסוק in ישעיהו was hinting at.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק in ישעיהו speaks about the king of אשור being 'shaved' by הקב"ה. The story gives a literal picture of that prophecy, with the beard itself destroyed.

keyTerms.meaning: This is what is written; this explains the פסוק
It will sweep away or destroy

phrases.english: They said: This is what is written:
phrases.notes: Some versions leave out the word in round brackets, so the line just reads 'This is what is written.'

phrases.english: "And it shall also sweep away the beard."
phrases.notes: ישעיהו 7:20

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Links the beard-burning story to a פסוק.
steps.raayaObject: The story of סנחריב's beard being burned off.

steps.title: רב פפא's popular saying about this story
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא says the folk saying about singeing a gentile comes from this story: if someone puts up with being mocked, the mockery only grows.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said: This is what people say: 'If you singe a gentile and he likes it, set fire to his beard, and you will never get tired of laughing at him.'
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא connects a well-known saying to the story of סנחריב's beard.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The saying means that if someone does not protest when he is mocked, the mockery will escalate. סנחריב put up with being humiliated, and it ended with his whole beard burned off.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב פָּפָּא, הַיְינוּ דְּאָמְרִי אִינָשֵׁי:
phrases.english: Rav Pappa said: This is what people say:
"If you singe a gentile and he finds it pleasant,
set fire to his beard
and you will never have your fill of laughing at him."

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב פָּפָּא, הַיְינוּ דְּאָמְרִי אִינָשֵׁי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a folk saying based on the same incident.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The saying about singeing a gentile's beard comes from סנחריב's story.

steps.title: סנחריב worships a plank from נח's תיבה and vows his sons
steps.stepSummary: סנחריב finds a plank from נח's תיבה, calls it the god that saved נח, and vows to sacrifice his two sons to it if he succeeds. His sons hear and kill him.
steps.simpleTranslation: He went and found a plank from נח's תיבה. He said: This is the great god who saved נח from the flood. He said: If that man (I) goes and succeeds, he will sacrifice his two sons before you. His sons heard and killed him.
steps.whatsHappening: The story reaches סנחריב's death. He makes an idol out of a plank from נח's תיבה, vows to sacrifice his sons to it, and they kill him first.
steps.deeperAnalysis: סנחריב thought the plank itself had saved נח, so he worshipped it. His vow to sacrifice his own sons is what led them to murder him.

phrases.english: He went and found a plank from Noah's ark.
He said: This is the great god
who saved Noah from the flood.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר: אִי אָזֵיל הָהוּא גַּבְרָא וּמַצְלַח,
phrases.english: He said: If that man goes and succeeds,
phrases.notes: 'That man' is סנחריב talking about himself.

phrases.english: he will sacrifice his two sons before you.
His sons heard and killed him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the shaving episode to סנחריב's death.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: סנחריב vowed to sacrifice his sons to a plank from the תיבה, and they killed him.

steps.title: The פסוק describing סנחריב's murder by his sons
steps.stepSummary: The פסוק in מלכים ב says סנחריב was killed by his sons while bowing in the house of נסרך his god. This fits the story.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is what is written: 'And it was, as he was bowing in the house of נסרך his god, that אדרמלך and שראצר his sons struck him with the sword...'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings the פסוק that matches the story: סנחריב's sons killed him while he worshipped his god.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The idol's name נסרך sounds like נסר, a plank. That supports the idea that his god was the plank from the תיבה. The פסוק also confirms that his own sons killed him.

keyTerms.meaning: Name of סנחריב's god, which sounds like נֶסֶר (plank)

phrases.english: This is what is written:
"And it came to pass, as he was bowing in the house of Nisroch his god,
phrases.notes: מלכים ב 19:37. The name נסרך sounds like נסר, a plank.

phrases.english: that Adrammelech and Sarezer his sons
struck him with the sword, etc."

steps.triggerLanguage: הַיְינוּ דִּכְתִיב: וַיְהִי הוּא מִשְׁתַּחֲוֶה בֵּית נִסְרֹךְ אֱלֹהָיו
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the death story with a פסוק.
steps.raayaObject: סנחריב's death at the hands of his sons while worshipping the plank.
steps.whatToRemember: סנחריב was humiliated (his beard burned off, as in ישעיהו) and then killed by his own sons while worshipping נסרך, which the גמרא reads as a plank from נח's תיבה.

steps.title: Introducing the פסוק about אברהם fighting 'by night'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the פסוק about אברהם splitting up against the kings 'לילה' in order to explain that word.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'And he divided himself against them by night, he and his servants, and struck them...'
steps.whatsHappening: This is a setup line. The גמרא quotes a פסוק about אברהם's war so that the next steps can explain the strange word 'לילה' in it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word 'לילה' seems extra in the פסוק. The two אמוראים in the next steps each explain why it is there.

keyTerms.meaning: Night, or here possibly a name

phrases.english: "And he divided himself against them by night,
phrases.notes: בראשית 14:15, about אברהם fighting the four kings.

phrases.english: he and his servants, and struck them, etc."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shifts from סנחריב to a related פסוק about אברהם's war.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Quotes the פסוק whose word 'לילה' will be explained.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן: לילה is the name of an angel
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן says 'לילה' is the name of the angel who helped אברהם, and he proves from איוב that there is an angel called לילה.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן said: The angel that came to help אברהם is named 'לילה,' as it says: 'And לילה said: A man-child has been conceived.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן reads 'לילה' as the name of an angel who fought alongside אברהם.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In איוב, 'לילה' speaks, so רבי יוחנן understands it as an angel. Here the פסוק means: אברהם and the angel לילה split up against the kings.

keyTerms.meaning: A male child has been conceived

phrases.english: Rabbi Yochanan said:
That angel who came to Abraham's aid,
"Laila" is his name,
as it is stated: "And Laila said: A man-child has been conceived."
phrases.notes: איוב 3:3

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן: אוֹתוֹ מַלְאָךְ שֶׁנִּזְדַּמֵּן לוֹ לְאַבְרָהָם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the first explanation of 'לילה'.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: 'לילה' is the name of the angel who helped אברהם.

steps.title: רבי יצחק נפחא: a night act, the stars fought for him
steps.stepSummary: רבי יצחק נפחא says 'לילה' means הקב"ה did a 'night act' for אברהם: the stars fought for him, like they fought against סיסרא.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יצחק נפחא said: He did a night act with him, as it says: 'From heaven they fought; the stars from their paths fought against סיסרא.'
steps.whatsHappening: A second אמורא gives a different explanation: 'לילה' means things of the night, the stars, fought on אברהם's side.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Instead of an angel named לילה, he reads 'לילה' as a description of how the help came: through the stars of the night. He brings the פסוק in שופטים as a proof that stars can fight for ישראל.

keyTerms.meaning: An act of night (done through the night sky)

phrases.english: And Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha said:
That He performed for him an act of night,
as it is stated: "From heaven they fought, the stars
phrases.notes: שופטים 5:20

phrases.english: from their courses fought against Sisera."

steps.triggerLanguage: וְרַבִּי יִצְחָק נַפָּחָא אָמַר: שֶׁעָשָׂה עִמּוֹ מַעֲשֵׂה לַיְלָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a different reading of 'לילה' than רבי יוחנן.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: 'לילה' means a night act: the stars fought for אברהם.

steps.title: ריש לקיש prefers רבי יצחק נפחא's explanation
steps.stepSummary: ריש לקיש says the explanation of the 'smith' (רבי יצחק נפחא) is better than that of the 'son of the smith' (רבי יוחנן).
steps.simpleTranslation: ריש לקיש said: The smith's explanation is better than the son of the smith's.
steps.whatsHappening: ריש לקיש weighs in on the מחלוקת and says he prefers רבי יצחק נפחא's reading over רבי יוחנן's.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He uses a play on words: רבי יצחק is 'נפחא,' the smith, and רבי יוחנן was known as 'בר נפחא,' son of the smith. ריש לקיש closes the discussion by favoring the stars explanation.

keyTerms.meaning: Son of the smith, a nickname of רבי יוחנן

steps.confusionAlert: 'נפחא' and 'בר נפחא' are two different people: 'נפחא' is רבי יצחק, and 'בר נפחא' is רבי יוחנן.

phrases.english: Reish Lakish said:
Better is the smith's statement than the son of the smith's.
phrases.notes: רבי יוחנן was known as 'בר נפחא,' son of the smith.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רֵישׁ לָקִישׁ: טָבָא דְּנַפָּחָא מִדְּבַר נַפָּחָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Judges between the two explanations of 'לילה'.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: ריש לקיש prefers רבי יצחק נפחא's reading that 'לילה' means the stars fought for אברהם.
steps.whatToRemember: There are two readings of 'לילה' in אברהם's war: רבי יוחנן says it is an angel named לילה, and רבי יצחק נפחא says the stars fought for him. ריש לקיש prefers the second.

steps.title: אברהם's strength weakened at Dan
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן explains 'וירדף עד דן': when אברהם reached דן his strength weakened, because he saw that his descendants would later worship idols there.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'And he chased them until דן.' רבי יוחנן says: once אברהם reached דן, he lost strength. He saw that his descendants would worship idols in דן, as the פסוק says ירבעם put one golden calf in בית אל and one in דן.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves on to the next words of the פסוק about אברהם's war with the kings. רבי יוחנן explains why it says אברהם chased them only 'until דן'.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The new idea is that a place can carry spiritual weight because of what will happen there in the future. אברהם lost strength at דן because ירבעם would later put a golden calf there. The proof is a פסוק in מלכים א.

phrases.english: "And he pursued as far as Dan."
phrases.notes: בראשית 14:14

phrases.english: Rabbi Yochanan says:

phrases.aramaic: כֵּיוָן שֶׁבָּא אוֹתוֹ צַדִּיק עַד דָּן,
phrases.english: Once that righteous one came to Dan,
phrases.notes: 'That righteous one' means אברהם.

phrases.english: his strength weakened.
He saw his descendants
who were destined to worship idols in Dan,
as it is stated:
"And he set one in Beit El,
and the other one he placed in Dan."
phrases.notes: מלכים א 12:29. This is about ירבעם's two golden calves.

steps.triggerLanguage: וַיִּרְדֹּף עַד דָּן אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues explaining the פסוק about אברהם's war with the kings, moving to the next words.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: אברהם weakened at דן because he foresaw his descendants' idol worship there.

steps.title: The wicked enemy also gained strength only at Dan
steps.stepSummary: The same idea works the other way: the wicked enemy only got the upper hand once he reached דן.
steps.simpleTranslation: And that wicked man too did not win until he reached דן, as the פסוק says: 'From דן the snorting of his horses is heard.'
steps.whatsHappening: The teaching about דן continues. Just as אברהם weakened there, the wicked enemy of ישראל only became strong when he reached דן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This shows the same point from the other side. The sin connected to דן weakened the righteous and strengthened the enemy. The proof is a פסוק in ירמיה.

phrases.english: And even that wicked one
phrases.notes: This is נבוכדנצר, who conquered ירושלים.

phrases.english: did not prevail until he reached Dan,
as it is stated: "From Dan the snorting of his horses is heard."
phrases.notes: ירמיה 8:16

steps.whatToRemember: דן is a place tied to the future idol worship. It weakened אברהם and gave strength to the enemy.
steps.triggerLanguage: וְאַף אוֹתוֹ רָשָׁע לֹא נִתְגַּבֵּר עַד שֶׁהִגִּיעַ לְדָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a matching example to רבי יוחנן's point about דן.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The enemy only overpowered ישראל once he reached דן.

steps.title: רבי זירא on the three warnings and what we tell people
steps.stepSummary: רבי זירא lists three warnings sent by רבי יהודה בן בתירא: respect an elder who forgot his learning, be careful with the veins in שחיטה, and respect the children of unlearned people. He says that even so, 'a matter like this' we do let them know.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי זירא says: רבי יהודה בן בתירא sent a message from נציבין: be careful to respect an old scholar who forgot his learning through no fault of his own, be careful about the veins like רבי יהודה, and be careful to respect the children of unlearned people, because Torah will come from them. Even so, a matter like this we tell them.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי זירא adds a side comment. He quotes three warnings from רבי יהודה בן בתירא and says that, in spite of them, there are certain things we still tell people.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The main warning here is the third one: do not look down on the children of עמי הארץ. רבי זירא's point is that even with that warning, a statement 'like this one' may still be said openly to them. The גמרא does not spell out here which statement he means.

keyTerms.meaning: An elder who forgot his learning

steps.confusionAlert: The middle warning about the veins is about שחיטה, not about people. It is listed here only because it was part of the same message from נציבין.

phrases.english: Rabbi Zeira says:
Even though there was sent
by Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira from Netzivin:
Be careful with an elder
who forgot his learning because of things beyond his control,
and be careful with the jugular veins, like Rabbi Yehuda,
phrases.notes: This is about שחיטה: cut the veins, as רבי יהודה holds.

phrases.english: and be careful with the children of unlearned people,
since Torah will come out from them —
a matter like this we do let them know.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי זֵירָא אַף עַל גַּב דְּשָׁלַח רַבִּי יְהוּדָה בֶּן בְּתֵירָא מִנְּצִיבִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A side comment that steps away from the פסוקים to say what may be told to people.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Even with the warning to respect the children of unlearned people, a matter like this one is still told to them.

steps.title: ירמיה asks why the wicked succeed
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes ירמיה's complaint to הקב"ה about why the wicked do well. Then it asks what answer Heaven gave him.
steps.simpleTranslation: ירמיה said: 'You are right, ה׳, if I argue with You, but still let me talk with You about justice: why do the wicked succeed and the traitors live in peace? You planted them, they took root, they grow and make fruit.' What did they answer him?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new topic by quoting ירמיה's famous question. It asks what Heaven answered, which sets up the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: ירמיה is not doubting that הקב"ה is fair. He opens by saying 'You are right'. Still, he wants to understand why the wicked do so well. The question 'מאי אהדרו ליה' tells us an answer is coming.

phrases.english: "Right are You, Lord, were I to argue with You;
yet I will speak with You about justice:
Why does the way of the wicked succeed,
why are all the traitors at ease?
You planted them, they even took root;
they grow, they even produce fruit."
phrases.notes: ירמיה 12:1-2

phrases.english: What did they answer him?
phrases.notes: 'They' means Heaven, answering ירמיה.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic: ירמיה's question about the success of the wicked.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What answer did Heaven give ירמיה's complaint?

steps.title: Heaven's answer: if people on foot tire you, how will you face horses?
steps.stepSummary: Heaven answers ירמיה with a פסוק: if running next to people on foot tired you out, how could you compete with horses?
steps.simpleTranslation: 'If you ran with people on foot and they wore you out, how will you race against horses? And if you only feel safe in a peaceful land, what will you do in the wild thickets of the ירדן?'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the answer to the question it just asked by quoting the next part of ירמיה. The answer is a picture: small challenges versus much bigger ones.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The answer does not explain directly why the wicked succeed. It uses a comparison of easy and hard tests. The next step will spell out the comparison with a parable.

keyTerms.meaning: The wild thickets of the ירדן

phrases.english: "If you ran with people on foot and they tired you out,
how will you compete with horses?
And in a land of peace you feel safe,
how will you manage in the wild thickets of the Jordan?"
phrases.notes: ירמיה 12:5

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question 'מאי אהדרו ליה' from step 14.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Heaven answers with a picture: if smaller challenges tire you, bigger ones will be much harder.

steps.title: The parable of the boastful runner
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains the פסוק with a parable. A man boasted he could outrun horses for three פרסאות in swampland, but he got tired after running three מיל on dry land next to a man on foot.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is like a man who said: 'I can run three פרסאות ahead of horses through swamps.' He met a man on foot, ran ahead of him three מיל on dry land, and got tired.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a parable to explain Heaven's answer to ירמיה. This step tells the story, and the next step draws the lesson.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Every detail of the boast is harder than what actually tired him out. He boasted about horses but tired against a man on foot. He boasted about פרסאות but tired after מילין. He boasted about swamps but tired on dry land. These three contrasts set up the three קל וחומר arguments that come next.

keyTerms.meaning: Parasangs, a long distance (four מיל each)

phrases.english: A parable of a man who said:
I can run three parasangs
phrases.notes: A פרסה is four מיל, so three פרסאות is four times the three מיל he actually ran.

phrases.english: ahead of the horses through the swamplands.
He came across a man on foot,
ran ahead of him three mil on dry land,
and got tired.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the פסוק from step 15 with a parable.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The פסוק is like a man who boasted about a hard run and then failed at an easy one.

steps.title: Three 'how much more so' lessons from the parable
steps.stepSummary: People tell the runner: if you got tired in the easy case, you would surely fail in the hard one. They say this three times: horses versus a man on foot, פרסאות versus מילין, and swamps versus dry land.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said to him: if you got this tired ahead of a man on foot, how much more ahead of horses! If three מיל did this to you, how much more three פרסאות! If dry land did this to you, how much more the swamps!
steps.whatsHappening: The parable ends with its lesson, given as three 'how much more so' arguments. This sets up the next step, where the גמרא applies the parable to ירמיה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each line is a קל וחומר: if the easier test was too much, the harder test surely will be. Together they explain the פסוק's message to ירמיה. If smaller things are already hard for you, the bigger ones will be much harder.

keyTerms.meaning: How much more so (a קל וחומר)
And if (opening a 'how much more so' argument)

steps.whatToRemember: Heaven answered ירמיה with a picture of easy versus hard tests. The parable spells it out with three קל וחומר arguments: horses, distance, and swampland.

phrases.english: They said to him:
If ahead of a man on foot you are like this,

phrases.aramaic: לִפְנֵי הַסּוּסִים – עַל אַחַת כַּמָּה וְכַמָּה.
phrases.english: ahead of the horses — how much more so!
And if three mil leave you like this,

phrases.aramaic: שָׁלֹשׁ פַּרְסָאוֹת – עַל אַחַת כַּמָּה וְכַמָּה.
phrases.english: three parasangs — how much more so!
And if on dry land you are like this,

phrases.aramaic: בֵּין בִּצְעֵי הַמַּיִם – עַל אַחַת כַּמָּה וְכַמָּה.
phrases.english: in the swamplands — how much more so!

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמְרוּ לוֹ וּמָה לִפְנֵי רַגְלִי כָּךְ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws the lesson from the parable in step 16.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: If the easy challenge tired him out, the hard one surely would be too much. This is the meaning of Heaven's answer to ירמיה.

steps.title: Applying the parable: if the wicked get reward, the אבות get far more
steps.stepSummary: Heaven tells ירמיה: if you are amazed at the reward I gave the wicked נבוכדנצר for four steps, think how much more I will reward אברהם יצחק ויעקב, who ran before Me like horses.
steps.simpleTranslation: So too you, ירמיה: if you are amazed at the reward I paid that wicked man for four steps he ran for My honor, then when I pay reward to אברהם, יצחק and יעקב, who ran before Me like horses, it will be so much greater!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא takes the runner parable from the last step and applies it straight to ירמיה's complaint.
steps.deeperAnalysis: ירמיה was bothered that the wicked do well. Heaven's answer is that their success is payment for small good deeds, like נבוכדנצר's four steps. If a small deed earns that much, the lifelong running of the אבות will earn far more, so ירמיה should not be shocked by the 'small' case.

keyTerms.meaning: all the more so, how much more

steps.whatToRemember: Even a small act done for God's honor earns real reward, even for a wicked person. So the reward of the righteous will be far greater.

phrases.english: So too, you:
phrases.notes: Heaven is now speaking to ירמיה, using the runner parable from before.

phrases.english: If regarding the reward for four steps
that I paid to that wicked man,
who ran for My honor,
you are amazed?
When I pay reward
to Avraham, Yitzchak and Yaakov,
who ran before Me like horses,
all the more so!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies the parable of the tired runner (Step 17) to ירמיה's question (Step 14).
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The wicked prosper because of small good deeds. The reward of the אבות will be much greater.

steps.title: ירמיה's reaction in a פסוק
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא shows this idea in a פסוק where ירמיה says his heart broke and he felt like a drunk man before God and His holy words.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is what is written: 'About the prophets: my heart is broken inside me, all my bones shake. I was like a drunk man, like a man overcome by wine, because of ה׳ and because of His holy words.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא links the answer just given to a פסוק describing how ירמיה felt.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The phrase 'היינו דכתיב' tells us this פסוק matches what was just taught. ירמיה is shaken, like a drunk man, because of God's words. In context, those words are Heaven's sharp answer to his complaint.

phrases.english: This is what is written:
"About the prophets, my heart is broken inside me,
phrases.notes: ירמיה 23:9

phrases.english: all my bones shake,
I was like a drunk man
and like a man whom wine has overcome,
because of ה׳ and because of His holy words."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Ties Heaven's answer to a פסוק about ירמיה's reaction.
steps.raayaObject: That ירמיה was shaken by Heaven's answer

steps.title: What were the four steps?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what event the 'four steps' of נבוכדנצר refers to.
steps.simpleTranslation: These four steps, what are they?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a question to set up the story behind נבוכדנצר's four steps.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 18 mentioned four steps that earned נבוכדנצר great reward, but never said what they were. Now the גמרא asks for the actual event.

phrases.english: These four steps, what are they?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks to explain the 'four steps' mentioned in Step 18.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which event the four steps of נבוכדנצר refers to

steps.title: The letter from the king of בבל
steps.stepSummary: The answer starts with a פסוק: מרודך בלאדן king of בבל sent letters to חזקיהו.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it is written: 'At that time מרודך בלאדן son of בלאדן, king of בבל, sent letters, and so on.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins its answer by quoting the פסוק where the story starts.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The four steps are connected to a letter the king of בבל sent to חזקיהו. The 'וגו׳' means the פסוק goes on: he sent letters and a gift, because he heard חזקיהו had been sick and got better.

keyTerms.meaning: and so on (the rest of the פסוק)

phrases.english: As it is written: "At that time
Merodach-Baladan son of Baladan sent
phrases.notes: ישעיהו 39:1

phrases.english: king of Babylonia, letters, and so on."
phrases.notes: The rest of the פסוק says he also sent a gift, because he heard חזקיהו had been sick and recovered.

steps.triggerLanguage: דִּכְתִיב בָּעֵת הַהִיא שָׁלַח מְרֹדַךְ בַּלְאֲדָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts answering the question of Step 20.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The four steps are part of the story of the letter מרודך בלאדן sent to חזקיהו.

steps.title: Would a king send gifts just because someone got well?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא wonders: just because חזקיהו was sick and recovered, the king of בבל sent him letters and a gift?
steps.simpleTranslation: Because 'חזקיהו was sick and got better' he sent him letters and a gift?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is surprised by the פסוק and asks why a foreign king would care so much about חזקיהו's recovery.
steps.deeperAnalysis: People get sick and recover all the time. Why would that make a far-off king send a gift? The question shows there must be something special behind this event.

phrases.english: Because "Hezekiah was sick and recovered,"
he sent him letters and a gift?

steps.triggerLanguage: מִשּׁוּם כִּי חָלָה חִזְקִיָּהוּ וַיֶּחֱזָק שַׁדַּר לֵיהּ סְפָרִים וּמִנְחָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the reason given in the פסוק quoted in Step 21.
steps.kashyaTarget: The reason in the פסוק for the king's letter
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A simple recovery from illness does not seem reason enough for a foreign king to send letters and a gift.

steps.title: Yes, because of the miracle
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers yes. He sent it to ask about the miracle that happened in the land, as another פסוק says.
steps.simpleTranslation: Yes, 'to ask about the wonder that happened in the land.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the recovery came with a great miracle, and that is what made the king write.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Another פסוק says the people of בבל came to ask about 'the wonder in the land.' So the letter was about a public miracle, not just a recovery. The next steps explain what that miracle was.

keyTerms.meaning: to ask about, to look into

phrases.english: Yes, "to ask about the wonder
phrases.notes: דברי הימים ב 32:31. Some versions have the word in round brackets and some don't.

phrases.english: that happened in the land."

steps.triggerLanguage: אִין לִדְרֹשׁ אֶת הַמּוֹפֵת אֲשֶׁר הָיָה בָאָרֶץ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 22.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Brings a second פסוק that gives the real reason
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The king wrote only because חזקיהו got well, which seems strange.
steps.terutzMaskana: The recovery came with a world-famous miracle, and the king wrote to ask about it.

steps.title: The day אחז died lasted only two hours
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן says that on the day חזקיהו's father אחז died, daylight lasted only two hours.
steps.simpleTranslation: As רבי יוחנן said: that day on which אחז died was only two hours long.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings רבי יוחנן to start explaining what the miracle was.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The miracle begins with a strange earlier event: the day אחז died was cut short by ten hours. This sets up the next step, where those hours are given back.

keyTerms.meaning: אחז, a wicked king, father of חזקיהו

phrases.english: As Rabbi Yochanan said:
That day on which Achaz died
was only two hours long.
phrases.notes: Daylight lasted just two hours, ten short of a normal day.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins explaining the 'wonder' mentioned in Step 23.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The day אחז died was shortened to two hours.

steps.title: The ten hours are given back to חזקיהו
steps.stepSummary: When חזקיהו recovered, הקב"ה gave him back the ten missing hours, as the פסוק says the sun went back ten steps.
steps.simpleTranslation: When חזקיהו was sick and got better, הקב"ה returned those ten hours to him. As it is written: 'I will turn back the shadow on the sundial of אחז ten steps backward. And the sun went back ten steps.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes describing the miracle: the sun went backward and the day grew longer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ten hours taken away on the day אחז died were returned when his son חזקיהו recovered. A long day like that would be seen around the world, which explains why the king of בבל noticed.

keyTerms.meaning: steps (here, the marks on a sundial)

phrases.english: And when Hezekiah was sick and recovered,
the Holy One, Blessed be He, returned
those ten hours to him,
as it is written: "Behold, I will turn back the shadow of the steps
phrases.notes: ישעיהו 38:8

phrases.english: that went down on the sundial of Achaz with the sun
backward ten steps."
"And the sun went back ten steps
on the steps it had gone down."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues רבי יוחנן's statement: the missing hours come back.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: When חזקיהו recovered, the ten lost hours were returned and the sun went backward.

steps.title: The king of בבל sends greetings
steps.stepSummary: מרודך בלאדן asks what happened, hears that חזקיהו recovered, and has a letter written greeting the king, the city and God, in that order.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to them: 'What is this?' They told him: 'חזקיהו was sick and got better.' He said: 'There is a man like this, and I should not send him greetings?' They wrote to him: 'Greetings to King חזקיהו, greetings to the city of ירושלים, greetings to the great God.'
steps.whatsHappening: The story moves to בבל: the king sees the long day, learns why, and sends a letter of greeting.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This shows why the king sent letters and a gift. Notice the order of the greetings: the king first and God last. That order is what the next step is about.

phrases.english: He said to them: What is this?
phrases.notes: "He" is מרודך בלאדן, the king of בבל, asking his servants about the long day.

phrases.english: They said to him: Hezekiah was sick and recovered.
He said: There is a man like this
and I should not send him greetings?
They wrote to him: "Greetings to King Hezekiah,
greetings to the city of Jerusalem,
greetings to the great God."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows how the miracle of Step 25 led to the letter from Step 21.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The king sent greetings to חזקיהו, ירושלים and God, with God named last.

steps.title: נבוכדנצר objects to God being named last
steps.stepSummary: נבוכדנצר, the king's scribe, was away when the letter was written. When he came back, he asked how it was written and objected that the 'great God' was put last.
steps.simpleTranslation: נבוכדנצר was בלאדן's scribe. At that time he was not there. When he came, he said to them: 'How did you write it?' They said: 'This is how we wrote.' He said: 'You call Him the great God, and you write Him last?'
steps.whatsHappening: נבוכדנצר enters the story and challenges the order of the greetings.
steps.deeperAnalysis: His point is simple logic: if you call Him 'the great God,' He should come first, not after a human king and a city. This objection is the start of his act of honoring God.

phrases.english: Nebuchadnezzar was Baladan's scribe.
At that time he was not there.

phrases.aramaic: כִּי אֲתָא, אֲמַר לְהוּ: הֵיכִי כָּתְבִיתוּ?
phrases.english: When he came, he said to them: How did you write it?
They said to him: This is how we wrote it.
He said to them: You call Him "the great God"
and you write Him last?

steps.triggerLanguage: קְרֵיתוּ לֵיהּ אֱלָהָא רַבָּא וְכָתְבִיתוּ לֵיהּ לְבַסּוֹף
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the order of greetings written in Step 26.
steps.kashyaTarget: The order of greetings in the letter
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Calling God 'great' while listing Him after a king and a city does not make sense.

steps.title: נבוכדנצר's corrected order
steps.stepSummary: נבוכדנצר says to write it the other way: greetings to God first, then the city, then the king.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said: 'Rather, write it like this: Greetings to the great God, greetings to the city of ירושלים, greetings to King חזקיהו.'
steps.whatsHappening: נבוכדנצר gives his fix for the letter, putting God first.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The new order is the exact reverse of the original. God now comes first and the human king last. This is the honor for God that נבוכדנצר stood up for.

phrases.english: He said: Rather, write it like this:
"Greetings to the great God,
greetings to the city of Jerusalem,
greetings to King Hezekiah."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the fix for the problem raised in Step 27.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Rewrites the letter in a new order
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The letter greets the king first and God last.
steps.terutzMaskana: The letter should greet God first and the king last.

steps.title: Let the one who read the letter be its messenger
steps.stepSummary: The other scribes tell נבוכדנצר: since you read the letter and objected, you be the messenger and fix it.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said to him: 'The one who reads the letter, let him be the messenger.'
steps.whatsHappening: The scribes put the job on נבוכדנצר: since he spoke up, he should carry out the fix himself.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This sets up נבוכדנצר's personal action for God's honor. It leads into the 'four steps' that Step 18 said earned him such great reward.

phrases.english: They said to him: The one who reads the letter,
let him be the messenger.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: The scribes respond to נבוכדנצר's correction in Step 28 by giving him the task.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: נבוכדנצר is made responsible for fixing the letter, which sets up his act of honoring God.

steps.title: נבוכדנצר runs after the messenger and is stopped by גבריאל
steps.stepSummary: נבוכדנצר runs after the messenger to fix the letter. After four steps, גבריאל stops him.
steps.simpleTranslation: He ran after the messenger. When he had run four steps, גבריאל came and stopped him.
steps.whatsHappening: The story goes on. נבוכדנצר takes on the job of fixing the letter and runs after the messenger, but the angel גבריאל stops him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 29 the other scribes told נבוכדנצר to be the messenger and fix the letter himself. Here he starts doing that by running. Heaven stops him after only four steps, so the effort he made for God's honor stays limited.

phrases.english: He ran after him,
phrases.notes: נבוכדנצר is running after the messenger who already left with the letter.

phrases.english: when he had run four steps,
Gabriel came and stopped him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Carries out what the scribes told him in step 29: he goes to fix the letter himself.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: נבוכדנצר ran four steps to honor God, and גבריאל stopped him.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן: had גבריאל not stopped him, ישראל would have been lost
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן says that if גבריאל had not stopped נבוכדנצר, there would have been no hope for ישראל.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן said: If גבריאל had not come and stopped him, there would have been no remedy for the enemies of ישראל.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן explains why it mattered that גבריאל stopped נבוכדנצר.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The reward for running to honor God would have grown with every step. If he had kept running, the reward would have given נבוכדנצר enough power to destroy ישראל completely. Stopping him early kept that reward small.

keyTerms.meaning: The enemies of ישראל, a polite way of saying ישראל itself

steps.confusionAlert: 'The enemies of ישראל' really means ישראל. The גמרא uses this phrase so it does not have to say something bad directly about the Jewish people.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yochanan said:
If Gabriel had not come and stopped him,
there would have been no remedy
for the enemies of Israel.
phrases.notes: This is a polite way to say 'for Israel.' The גמרא avoids saying something bad about ישראל directly.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן: אִילְמָלֵא לֹא בָּא גַּבְרִיאֵל וְהֶעֱמִידוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains why it mattered that גבריאל stopped נבוכדנצר in step 30.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Without גבריאל stopping him, נבוכדנצר's reward would have let him destroy ישראל.
steps.whatToRemember: Even a small act of honoring God earns a huge reward. נבוכדנצר's four steps were already very powerful, so Heaven had to stop him.

steps.title: Why is he called 'בלאדן son of בלאדן'?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the פסוק gives both the king and his father the name בלאדן.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the meaning of 'בלאדן son of בלאדן'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a question about the name of the king in the story, מרודך בלאדן. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק says 'מרודך בלאדן son of בלאדן,' so the son seems to carry his father's name as his own. The גמרא wants to know why the son is called by his father's name.

keyTerms.meaning: בלאדן son of בלאדן, the king's name in the פסוק

phrases.english: What is "Baladan son of Baladan"?
phrases.notes: ישעיה 39:1. The son and the father both seem to be called בלאדן, so the גמרא asks why.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the story for a moment to explain the king's name from the פסוק quoted in step 21.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why the son and the father share the name בלאדן.

steps.title: The son ruled for his dog-faced father and signed the father's name
steps.stepSummary: The father בלאדן's face turned like a dog's, so his son ruled instead. The son still signed his father's name as king, which fits 'a son honors his father.'
steps.simpleTranslation: They say: בלאדן was a king, and his face changed and became like a dog's. His son sat on the throne instead. Whenever the son wrote a letter, he wrote his own name and his father's name, 'King בלאדן.' This is what the פסוק means: 'A son honors his father and a servant his master.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question: the son kept his father's name in his signature to honor him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The father could no longer rule because his face had changed. The son became king, but he still wrote his father's name as 'King בלאדן.' The גמרא ties this to the פסוק in מלאכי as an example of 'a son honors his father.'

phrases.english: They say:
Baladan was a king,
and his face changed
and became like that of a dog.
His son sat on the throne.
When he would write,
he would write his own name and his father's name,
"King Baladan."
That is what is written:
"A son honors his father and a servant his master."
phrases.notes: מלאכי 1:6

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 32.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The son ruled in place of his disfigured father and still signed 'King בלאדן' to honor him. That is why he is called 'son of בלאדן' with the same name.
steps.whyThisMatters: It links the story to the פסוק in מלאכי, which the גמרא goes on to explain half by half.

steps.title: Explaining both halves of the פסוק: the son and the servant
steps.stepSummary: 'A son honors his father' is the בלאדן story. 'A servant his master' is shown with a פסוק about נבוזראדן, נבוכדנצר's officer, at the burning of the בית המקדש.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'A son honors his father' is what we just said. 'And a servant his master' is as it is written: 'And in the fifth month, on the tenth of the month, which was the nineteenth year of King נבוכדנצר, king of Babylon, נבוזראדן, captain of the guard, who stood before the king of Babylon, came into Jerusalem and burned the House of ה׳ and the house of the king.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes through the פסוק in מלאכי one half at a time. For the 'servant' half, it brings a פסוק in ירמיה about נבוזראדן. This sets up an explanation that comes right after.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first half is already covered by the בלאדן story. For the second half, the source is a פסוק saying נבוזראדן 'stood before the king of Babylon in Jerusalem.' The גמרא has not yet explained how that phrase shows a servant honoring his master. That explanation comes next.

keyTerms.meaning: נבוכדנצר's chief officer, who burned the בית המקדש
